title: When not to use regex
summary: CSV with quoted fields, URLs, HTML, XML, JSON and email addresses: why a regex breaks on each, and the parser a senior reaches for instead.

steps.title: Some formats have state
body: Below, the pattern `,` finds every comma. Splitting on them gives five fields on the first line, not four:
`"Acme, Inc."` is **one** field. In CSV (RFC 4180) a quoted field can hold commas, doubled quotes (`""` means one
`"`) and even line breaks. Whether a comma separates fields depends on how many quotes came before it on the
line, and possibly on earlier lines. That is state, and a parser tracks it for you.
The same goes for other formats you meet every week:
- **HTML and XML** nest to any depth, attributes come in any order, and HTML has optional closing tags. A regex
cannot count nesting.
- **JSON** nests, allows any key order and escapes characters (`\u0022` is a quote).
- **URLs** have schemes, user info, ports, percent-encoding and international host names.
Rule of thumb: if the format has a grammar and a parser in the standard library, use the parser. Use a regex for
flat text with a fixed shape: log lines, ids, dates, versions.

steps.explain: `Split(',')` knows nothing about quotes, so `"Acme` and ` Inc."` become two fields and the price moves to index 3. An importer that reads the price from index 2 now stores ` Inc."` as the price, or crashes trying to parse it.

steps.title: Symptom: "Inc." ended up in the price column
prompt: **Symptom.** After last night's customer import, the company of order 42 is `"Acme` and its price is ` Inc."`. The
importer splits each line on commas.
Fix `List<string> Companies(string csv)`: return the `company` column (the second field) of every data row, without
the header, with quotes handled properly. Use the CSV parser that ships with .NET:
```csharp
using var parser = new TextFieldParser(new StringReader(csv));
parser.SetDelimiters(",");
parser.HasFieldsEnclosedInQuotes = true;
string[]? fields = parser.ReadFields();   // one record; null at the end
// loop while !parser.EndOfData
`TextFieldParser` (namespace `Microsoft.VisualBasic.FileIO`, imported for you) is in the base library and fine for
small jobs. Real projects usually use **CsvHelper** from NuGet, which maps rows to classes; Python has the `csv`
module and PowerShell has `Import-Csv`.
solution: using var parser = new TextFieldParser(new StringReader(csv));
template: Dojo.Eq("quoted commas and doubled quotes", new List<string> { "Acme, Inc.", "The \"Best\" Shop", "Contoso" }, Companies(dojoCsv));
Dojo.Eq("a header with no rows", new List<string>(), Companies("id,company,total\n"));
hints: Read the header once with `parser.ReadFields();` and ignore it. Then loop `while (!parser.EndOfData)`.
Inside the loop: `var fields = parser.ReadFields()!; result.Add(fields[1]);`

steps.title: Use the parser that already exists
body: | Data | Reach for | Why a regex breaks |
| CSV | `TextFieldParser`, **CsvHelper**, Python `csv`, `Import-Csv` | quotes, `""`, line breaks inside fields |
| HTML | **AngleSharp** (CSS selectors) or **HtmlAgilityPack** | nesting, optional tags, attribute order, entities |
| XML | `XDocument` / `XmlReader` | nesting, namespaces, CDATA, entities |
| JSON | `System.Text.Json` (`JsonDocument`, `JsonSerializer`) | nesting, escapes, any key order |
| URL | `Uri.TryCreate` | user info, ports, percent-encoding, IDN hosts |
| Email | a loose shape check, then a confirmation email | see below |
`System.Uri` gives you the parts, already normalised:
```csharp
if (Uri.TryCreate(input, UriKind.Absolute, out var uri) && uri.Scheme == Uri.UriSchemeHttps)
Console.WriteLine($"{uri.Host} {uri.Port} {uri.AbsolutePath} {uri.Query}");
**Email.** The RFC 5322 address grammar allows quoted local parts, comments and more; the famous "complete" regex
for it runs to thousands of characters and still rejects or accepts the wrong things. Worse, a valid address may not
exist. Teams check a loose shape (one `@`, text on both sides, no spaces) and then **send a confirmation email**:
only a click on that link proves the address. `MailAddress.TryCreate` exists, but it also accepts display-name forms
like `Bob <bob@contoso.com>`, so compare its `Address` with the input if you use it.

steps.prompt: Match each input to the tool a senior would parse it with.
pairs: A product page scraped for prices
A callback URL from a partner
A CSV export from the finance system
steps.explain: The last one is the regex's home ground: flat text, one record per line, a fixed shape.

`Uri` lower-cases the scheme and host (they are case-insensitive), fills in the default port when there is none (443 for https), and `Query` keeps its leading `?`. For the individual query values, use `System.Web.HttpUtility.ParseQueryString(u.Query)` or `QueryHelpers` in ASP.NET Core.

steps.prompt: You are reviewing the signup form. Which email check should ship?
options: A loose shape check (one `@`, text on both sides, no spaces), then a confirmation email with a link
The full RFC 5322 regex from Stack Overflow, and no confirmation
No check at all: just store what the user typed
steps.explain: A strict regex rejects real users (`o'brien@example.ie`, `first.last+tag@sub.contoso.co.uk`) and still accepts addresses that do not exist. The loose check catches typos such as a missing `@`; the confirmation email proves the address works. Storing anything at all lets bots fill your table.

steps.title: A loose email shape
prompt: Write the loose check: the whole input is one or more characters that are not `@` or whitespace, then `@`, then a
domain of non-`@`, non-whitespace characters that contains at least one dot with text on both sides.
It should accept `o'brien@example.ie` and `first.last+tag@sub.contoso.com`, and refuse `a@b`, `a b@c.com` and
`a@b@c.com`.
hints: "Not `@` and not whitespace" is the negated class `[^@\s]`.
steps.explain: Negated classes keep it short, strict about the one thing that matters (exactly one `@`, no spaces) and linear in time. The confirmation email does the rest.

steps.title: Where does this URL really point?
prompt: Partners register webhook URLs, and the ops dashboard shows where each one points. Write
`string Endpoint(string url)`: for an absolute `http` or `https` URL return `host:port`, otherwise return `invalid`.
Use `Uri.TryCreate` and the `Host` and `Port` properties; no regex.
| url | result |
| `https://api.contoso.com/v1/orders` | `api.contoso.com:443` |
| `http://localhost:5000/health` | `localhost:5000` |
| `https://user:pw@api.contoso.com/` | `api.contoso.com:443` |
| `ftp://files.contoso.com/a.zip` | `invalid` |
| `not a url` | `invalid` |
Check the scheme explicitly: on Linux and macOS, `Uri.TryCreate("/relative/path", UriKind.Absolute, ...)` succeeds
as a `file://` URI.
solution: if (!Uri.TryCreate(url, UriKind.Absolute, out var uri)) return "invalid";
template: Dojo.Eq("user info is not the host", "api.contoso.com:443", Endpoint("https://user:pw@api.contoso.com/"));
Dojo.Eq("a look-alike host is shown as it really is", "api.contoso.com.evil.io:443", Endpoint("https://api.contoso.com.evil.io/"));
Dojo.Eq("text is refused", "invalid", Endpoint("not a url"));
Dojo.Eq("a relative path is refused", "invalid", Endpoint("/relative/path"));
steps.explain: A regex like `https://([^/]+)` would report `user:pw@api.contoso.com` as the host. `Uri` knows the grammar, so the look-alike `api.contoso.com.evil.io` is shown for what it is.
